note: Kapitel 4, Teil 1 – Erkundung im Archivkeller und im Dienststollen 3 unter dem Güterbahnhof Karsk (Alexei) und an der Wendeschleife Süd 8 und in der Nebenstelle Süd (Konrad), die Aufgabe „Ilses Puppe“ und das Minispiel „Der Hebelrahmen“. Funde in der Stimme dessen, der sie erreichen kann. Daten: data/explore/c4_tunnels.json, c4_annex.json; Karten zur realen Geschichte: de_history_c4.json.

strings.ui.explore.place.L_C4_AnnexA: Süd 8 turning loop and South Branch
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.sugar_mouse.title: A guest under the shelf
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.sugar_mouse.text: Under the bottom shelf a field mouse sits in front of a sugar cube as big as its head. It has rolled it all the way from the table, right across the archive. It looks at me and doesn’t move. We both come at night, we both take what’s left over, and neither of us is in the duty book.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.stamps.title: The stamp box
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.stamps.text: At the end of the shelf, a stamp box, each stamp on its hook: “Принято” – accepted, “Отправлено” – dispatched, “Порожний” – empty, “Переадресовано” – rebooked. One hook is empty. On the wood beneath, the impression is still there: “Отдел Т”, Department T. Whoever took that one didn’t want anyone else using it.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.card_index.title: Personnel index
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.card_index.text: The goods office personnel index. Most cards are dull, as they should be. One is not: “Gerassimow, P. – pointsman, signal box 2 – transferred at own request, 3.2.1964.” Beneath, small, in pencil: “asked about wagon 24 318”. Whoever asks gets rebooked too. I’ve been asking for weeks.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.lev_photo.title: A photo by the lamp
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.lev_photo.text: Leaning against the lamp base, a photo: a girl of eighteen in front of a colonnade, holding a Leningrad University leaflet. On the back, in Lev’s hand: “Mascha. Rejected, 1963. Questionnaire, line 14.” I don’t need to ask what line 14 says. Whoever was in captivity is in it – and everyone who comes after him.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.samovar.title: Two glasses
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.samovar.text: The samovar is still humming. Beside it, two tea glasses in tin holders, one half empty, one full and cold, with a skin on top. Lev always pours two, even at night – for a visitor who doesn’t come. I don’t ask who it is. In Karsk you don’t ask about people who don’t come.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.stove.title: The stove in the vault
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.stove.text: A pot-bellied stove, its pipe running across the vault to the open air. On the plate a kettle; beside it, felt boots with galoshes are drying. In the ash box, edges of printed forms, not quite burned: “Опросный лист репатрианта”, questionnaire for returnees, a whole stack, blank. Lev heats the place with forms he once had to fill in himself. They burn badly. But they give warmth.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.air_raid_sign.text: Beside the iron door, an enamel sign: “Бомбоубежище – Служебный тоннель №3”, air-raid shelter, service tunnel 3. Below it, an arrow and, smaller: “Вместимость 400 чел.” – four hundred persons. The bombers never got as far as Karsk. They built it anyway, and well. What is well built always finds a new use.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.title: Lev at his table
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.text: Lev explains the iron door to me, and a set of points that sticks in winter – it really is in the duty book. And the second glass of tea was for me.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.l1: The door’s been stiff since forty-one. Don’t pull, Morozov – lift, then push. Otherwise it squeals all the way to the signal box.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.l2: You know the tunnel well for an archivist.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.l3: I know every door in this building. The ones you get in by, and the ones you get out by.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.l4: And if someone sees me down there?
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.l5: Then you’re an engineer checking W2. It really does stick in winter, it’s even in the duty book.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.chat_lev.l7: And drink your tea first. The second glass has been standing there since four. For you, as it turns out.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.field_phone.title: Field telephone in the niche
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.field_phone.text: In a niche, a field telephone from 1941, wooden case, crank. The line is live. I lift the receiver: a woman’s voice, tired and precise: “Карск-Сортировочная, семь часов тридцать две.” Somewhere up above, someone announces the time every minute – for a tunnel with no clock and officially no one who would need one. I hang up quietly.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.cables.title: New cables on old hooks
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.cables.text: On the hooks from 1941 hang the old cables, cloth and tar, long dead. Beside them, freshly clamped, a black rubber cable stamped “1963”, for the cage lamps and the pump at the end of the tunnel. A tunnel that is no longer on any plan is getting new cables. Someone wrote an application for that, and someone approved it. Verbally, I expect.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.lever_frame.title: The lever frame at W2
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.lever_frame.text: Eight levers, cast frame 1941, the locks freshly greased. Two routes have a label: entry track 1, exit main line. Lever 6 has none, only a handle worn shiny. Its route leads not onto the main line but onto a track with no number: “Кордон 17”. That’s why the wagons are missing from the signal-box register. I put every lever back the way I found it.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.child_drawing.text: A stack of rough bench planks, taken out of a wagon, for the next run. A house is scratched into the top plank with a nail, at a child’s height: a roof, four windows, a chimney with smoke. There was a name underneath, but someone has scraped it off with a knife. The house they left. Houses bother nobody.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.stovepipes.title: Stovepipes and buckets
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.stovepipes.text: Stovepipe elbows, a small iron stove, zinc buckets, brackets for benches. A kit that turns a goods wagon into a wagon for people. I know it from every textbook on wagon building: the teplushka. On old wagons the stencil for it read: “40 человек, 8 лошадей” – forty people or eight horses. The textbooks say how many fit in a wagon. Where it goes, they never say.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.painters_corner.te: A crate for a table, three tea glasses, a crust of bread, Wednesday’s “Gudok”, folded at the page with the plan targets. On the post, a duty roster: “Work column 7 – Sunday from 08:00 – painting and lettering, track 1”. No names, only numbers from 1 to 9. The men who paint numbers on the wagons here have numbers themselves.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.plate_heap.title: A heap of wagon plates
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.plate_heap.text: Enamel plates, a whole heap, each with a wagon number: 24 301, 24 307, 24 311, 24 322 … Twelve numbers from the same series, all “under repair” according to the stock book. I haven’t seen a single one of these wagons in a workshop this winter. Here their numbers lie in a heap, and the wagons run under others.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.wagon_marks.title: Markings on the solebar
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.wagon_marks.text: On the solebar, the markings every wagon carries: home depot, last inspection, next due date. “Карск, 11.1962.” Beneath it, painted over and still legible: “Исключён из инвентаря, 03.1963” – withdrawn from stock. A wagon that hasn’t existed for a year stands freshly painted on track 1. Nobody looks for a wagon that doesn’t exist.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.exit_portal.title: The exit gate
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.exit_portal.text: The gate to the main line, two leaves of sheet steel, a padlock as big as my fist, new. Grey light falls through the cracks; the wind smells of snow and coal. Outside lies Karsk, my signal box, my line. From down here it looks like a line on which things run at night that I have never seen.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_beam.title: Names on the roof beam
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_beam.text: At the end of the wagon, a vent flap, hardly bigger than a book. I pull myself up and look in: names on the roof beam, written in stove soot, as high as a person can reach standing. “Ольга Т.” – Olga T. “Hermann B.” “Нина, 17”. Three. I write them in my notebook, letter by letter. Further along, by the stovepipe, the wood is darker still.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_pipe.title: Behind the stovepipe
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_pipe.text: The stovepipe goes through a hole in the roof; the metal around it is sooted. Behind it, where it was warmest, four names scratched with a nail: “Мария Г.”, “Lena, 4”, “Мирон, 6” and above them, larger, “Wilhelm S.” The children sat by the stove, and someone made sure they didn’t touch the metal. There are scratches under the bench by the door too.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_bench.title: Under the bench
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_bench.text: I lie down on the planks and look under the front bench. Where no lamp reaches, someone wrote lying down, small and crooked: “Григорий Н.”, “Emma W.”, “Фёдор”, “Käthe R.” Beside them seven strokes, one across them all: a week. Whoever lay down here counted the days. That leaves the door. On its runner the paint is scratched.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_rail.title: On the door runner
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_rail.text: The runner of the sliding door, freshly painted outside. Inside, where the door strikes when it opens, the paint is scratched down to the iron: “Алла П.”, “Otto M.”, “Тамара С.” and a date, 21.1. Three, four, four, three. Fourteen, as it says on the plank inside. My notebook now has a page that is in no freight ledger. Lev should see it.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.title: Fourteen names
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.text: I show Lev the fourteen names from the wagon. He reads them half aloud, in both scripts, and copies them into his own notebook with the pencil from behind his ear.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.l1: Lev. There are names in the wagon – on the beam, behind the stovepipe, under the bench, on the door runner. I copied them down.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.l2: Show me. … Ольга Т. Hermann B. Нина, seventeen. Lena, four. Мирон, six.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.l3: Fourteen. And in our books the wagon ran empty.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.l4: “Empty” is a stamp, Morozov. It hangs in my box, right next to “Rebooked”.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.l5: Hold still, I’m copying them. My pencil can do both scripts.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.l6: You’re copying them? You didn’t want to be in any paper.
strings.explore.karsk.tunnels.names_lev.l7: Me, Morozov. Not them. Fourteen. Now they’re in two papers.
strings.task.karsk.fourteen.title: We are fourteen
strings.task.karsk.fourteen.summary: In wagon 24 318, people scratched their names into the wood and wrote them in soot. I want to read every one before the wagon runs again on Tuesday.
strings.task.karsk.fourteen.hint.beam: The vent at the left end of the wagon: something is written on the roof beam.
strings.task.karsk.fourteen.hint.pipe: Behind the stovepipe, where the wood is darkest.
strings.task.karsk.fourteen.hint.bench: Under the front bench, through the half-open door.
strings.task.karsk.fourteen.hint.rail: On the runner of the sliding door.
strings.task.karsk.fourteen.hint.lev: Take the fourteen names to Lev, who is keeping watch at the end of the wagon.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.house_11.title: Number eleven
strings.explore.berlin.annex.house_11.text: Number eleven is still lived in. On the first floor a desk lamp with a green shade is burning; between the double windows, a geranium that won’t survive the winter. Marta’s window. On my site plan, eleven is hatched like all the others: “to be cleared, second section”. I drew the hatching myself, with a ruler, without lifting the pen.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_shoe.title: A red shoe
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_shoe.text: By the step of number nine, half in the snow, a doll’s shoe, red, no bigger than my thumbnail. The clearance took everything that could be given a number. None could be found for this shoe. I put it on the window ledge, where it can be seen from the tram.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.wallpaper.title: Three floors of wallpaper
strings.explore.berlin.annex.wallpaper.prompt: Look at the open number nine
strings.explore.berlin.annex.wallpaper.text: Above the boarded-up door the front of number nine has been taken down; the house shows three floors in section: brown flowers, blue stripes, and at the top pale rectangles where pictures hung. In the middle, in the Lindners’ room facing the street, a towel still hangs on a nail, white, with red cross-stitch. It was nailed down, so it stayed. Anna came from Kharkov in forty-two, with a transport. She hadn’t brought much.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.shelter_poster.text: On the tram shelter, a poster: a crane, the dome, three workers with open shirts, sunshine. “Berlin builds – your contribution to the axis”. The corner is torn off; underneath, someone has written in pencil: “and where do we live?” The perspective is wrong, the dome is too close. Only a draughtsman would notice. Everyone else notices the pencil.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.tram_cab.title: Marta’s cab
strings.explore.berlin.annex.tram_cab.text: Through the cab window: the controller handle, worn shiny, a hook for the route board, a thermos whose smell of coffee comes through the cracks. On the dashboard, a child’s mitten, blue, with a white snowflake. Marta drives with a mitten behind the windscreen so that a certain eight-year-old knows which tram is hers.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.title: Marta at the loop
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.text: Marta has driven the 74 since 1955. The line used to run straight; now it curves around holes. Paul Lindner’s monthly pass is still in her pocket.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.l1: Four more minutes. If you must freeze, Mr Draughtsman, at least do it out of the wind.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.l2: How long have you been driving this line?
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.l3: Since fifty-five. Back then the 74 still ran straight. Now I drive in curves around holes.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.l4: And the people from the holes?
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.l5: They don’t ride with me any more. The monthly passes expire. I’ve still got one of Paul Lindner’s in my pocket.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_marta.l7: Because it’s valid till the end of February. Till then he’s a passenger. After that we’ll see.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_ask.title: Marta’s request
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_ask.text: Ilse hasn’t slept since January. Her doll was left behind in the sealed number nine. The cellars of eleven and nine have been connected since the war.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_ask.l1: Herr Adler – one more thing. Ilse can’t sleep. Her doll was left in number nine, in the kitchen on the bench.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_ask.l3: The front door, yes. But the cellars are connected, since the war. At ours in number eleven there’s a breach at the back, only loosely bricked up.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_ask.l4: An air-raid breach. It’s on my site plan. I drew it in myself.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_ask.l5: Then you know which way to go. Everyone here knows me. You’re just a gentleman with a briefcase.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_cellar.title: The breach
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_cellar.text: In the cellar of number eleven, behind the coal, the white lettering from forty-one: “Breach”. Three courses of bricks without mortar. Beyond, the stairs of number nine, and upstairs, at the back facing the yard, the Lindners’ kitchen, still intact. A chalk number on every piece of furniture, the clearance inventory, neatly up to 64. The doll sits on the bench with no number; it is missing a red shoe. A child’s drawing hangs on the wall. I take both.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.title: The doll
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.text: Ilse’s drawing shows number nine with all its windows lit. All windows lit means: everyone is at home. What has no number, nobody collects.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.l1: The doll. And you’ve come back cleaner than I thought you would.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.l2: There was a drawing on the wall. Number nine, all the windows lit.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.l3: She drew that in December. All the windows lit means: everyone’s at home.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.l4: In the kitchen every chair has a number. Only the doll hasn’t.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.l5: Then that’s how it stays. What has no number, nobody collects.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.doll_back.l7: She lost it in January, that morning. Thank you, Herr Adler. Tonight she’ll sleep.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.tram_rear.title: The back seat
strings.explore.berlin.annex.tram_rear.text: In the 74’s last window sits a girl, satchel on her lap, drawing with her finger on the misted glass: a house, four windows. When she notices me looking, she wipes it away. Children who are hidden learn quickly what to wipe away.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.axis_view.title: A gap in the hoarding
strings.explore.berlin.annex.axis_view.text: “Building site – No entry”. Through a gap between two boards, the open space: survey stakes with red-and-white flags, the cranes of the axis, the dome far behind. I wrote the coordinates of every stake into a table. On paper it was an area. From here it is cellar holes with scraps of wallpaper and a carpet-beating rail with a clothes peg.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.fans.title: Two fans
strings.explore.berlin.annex.fans.text: Behind the grille two fans are turning, each bigger than a man. On the brass plate: “Ventilation, South Branch – design: General Building Office, sheet 3”. My sheet. I calculated the air requirement, so many cubic metres for so many people per hour. I thought they were people who worked here. They are cards too. Cards don’t breathe, but they have to be kept dry.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.brandt_card.title: A card sticking up
strings.explore.berlin.annex.brandt_card.text: Drawer Süd 3 stands a finger’s breadth open; a card sticks out: “Brandt, W., architectural draughtsman, General Building Office. Flat Süd 3, vacated 3.1963. Note: transferred to State Police.” In the margin, in pencil: “Informant: colleague”. No name. “They don’t count rooms, they count addresses,” he left me. Who counted him, he didn’t know.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.household_index.tex: Above the drawers, an enamel sign: “Household Index Süd”, and below, small, the order: “Route – street – house number. Children on supplementary sheet.” The children come last, after the house number, on a sheet of their own. Twelve drawers, one for each section of route 74. Nobody here looks for people. They look for addresses, and the people hang from them.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.card_cart.title: The card trolley
strings.explore.berlin.annex.card_cart.text: A card trolley on rubber wheels, the compartments full, each bundle with a rubber band and a routing slip: “Handover Kordon – Tue 18 Feb, late shift until 24:00”. On the top slip someone has written in pencil: “Frl. Kunze’s birthday – cake!” There will be cake, on Tuesday, on the late shift.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.waiting_bench.title: Wait until called
strings.explore.berlin.annex.waiting_bench.text: A wooden bench, above it the sign “Wait until called” and a number display showing 17. At six in the morning nobody is waiting here. The bench stands beside the door to the State Police corridor, not beside the exit. It is for those who are brought here. I don’t sit down.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.perforator.title: The perforating machine
strings.explore.berlin.annex.perforator.text: At the end of the counter, a cast-iron perforating machine with a long lever, half a card in its jaws. A brass plate names the operation: “Perforate C-17 cards down the middle and separate. Left half: Reich. Right half: counterpart office.” Every card is divided between two countries before the person on it leaves one. The teeth only fit together if you have both halves.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.title: The corridor guard
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.text: The guard in front of the corridor to the State Police. This is no exit, he says, this is the corridor. And it gets written down all the same.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.l1: Good morning. Is this the way to the street?
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.l2: This is no exit. This is the corridor.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.l3: And where does the corridor lead?
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.l4: To people who ask more questions than you. The ladder’s back there.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.l5: Thank you. I lost my way.
strings.explore.berlin.annex.chat_guard.l6: They all say that here. It gets written down all the same.
strings.task.berlin.doll.title: Ilse’s doll
strings.task.berlin.doll.summary: Ilse has hardly slept since January. Her doll was left behind in the Lindners’ sealed flat, on the bench in the kitchen.
strings.task.berlin.doll.hint.ask: Hear what Marta asks of you at the loop.
strings.task.berlin.doll.hint.cellar: The cellars of eleven and nine are connected. The cellar entrance is to the left of number eleven’s front door.
strings.task.berlin.doll.hint.back: Bring Marta the doll before the 74 leaves.
strings.mg.lever.title: The lever frame
strings.mg.lever.subtitle: A lever frame from 1941, the locks freshly greased. Tucked into the frame is the night shift’s train register: three orders, in pencil.
strings.mg.lever.instruction: Carry out the three orders: first the points, then the route, last the signal – and back in reverse order.
strings.mg.lever.order.entry: Entry from the tunnel to track 1: route a, then signal 1.
strings.mg.lever.order.main: Exit from track 1 to the main line: route b, then signal 2. Release the entry first.
strings.mg.lever.order.zero: The third order names no route, only a lever: number 6, unlabelled. Then signal 2.
strings.mg.lever.table.title: Locking table
strings.mg.lever.desc.w1: At the tunnel mouth. Normal (+): track 1, reverse (−): track 2.
strings.mg.lever.desc.w2: At the exit end. Normal (+): track 1, reverse (−): track 2.
strings.mg.lever.desc.w3: In front of the gate. Normal (+): main line, reverse (−): the track with no number.
strings.mg.lever.desc.a: Entry from the tunnel to track 1. Locks points 1.
strings.mg.lever.desc.b: Exit from track 1 to the main line. Locks points 1, 2 and 3.
strings.mg.lever.desc.c: No label, the handle worn shiny. Locks points 1, 2 and 3.
strings.mg.lever.desc.s1: Home signal at the tunnel. Clears only with route a set.
strings.mg.lever.desc.s2: Starting signal at track 1. Clears only with route b or c set.
strings.mg.lever.fail.points_locked: {w} is locked – route {r} holds it. Release the route first.
strings.mg.lever.fail.route_points: Route {r} cannot be set: {w} must be {lage}.
strings.mg.lever.fail.route_conflict: Route {r} excludes {o} – both leave track 1 over points 2. Release {o} first.
strings.mg.lever.fail.route_held: Route {r} is locked by {s}. Put the signal back to stop first.
strings.mg.lever.fail.signal_no_route: {s} is stuck: without a set route the frame won’t release the signal.
strings.mg.lever.status.start: Eight levers, and none bears more than a number. The frame explains itself if you let it.
strings.mg.lever.status.restart: Everything back as the night shift left it.
strings.mg.lever.status.already_back: Lever {n} is already in the normal position.
strings.mg.lever.done.entry: Signal 1 shows clear. The entry to track 1 is free.
strings.mg.lever.done.main: Signal 2 shows clear. The exit to the main line is free.
strings.mg.lever.done.zero: Signal 2 shows clear. The indicator lights up: “КОРДОН 17”.
strings.mg.lever.solved: Track 0 – “Кордон 17”. No wagon from here runs over the main line. That is why none is in the signal-box register.
strings.mg.lever.hint.1: Tip: set the points as the locking table requires, then the route, then the signal. Back: signal, route, points.
strings.mg.vent.title: The ventilation dampers
strings.mg.vent.subtitle: Behind the grille the fault bell is ringing. Two fans, three ducts, three dampers on the desk – and on the wall my own sheet 3 with the air volumes.
strings.mg.vent.instruction: Set the dampers so that each duct gets its air volume from sheet 3. Every damper moves all three needles. When all are in the green zone, acknowledge the fault.
strings.mg.vent.sheet.title: Sheet 3 · Air volumes
strings.mg.vent.status.start: The bell is ringing. The night shift has been turning the dampers.
strings.mg.vent.status.restart: The dampers are back as the night shift left them.
strings.mg.vent.status.balanced: All three needles in the green zone. Now acknowledge the fault.
strings.mg.vent.fail.low: The bell keeps ringing: duct {n} – {name} is getting too little air.
strings.mg.vent.fail.high: The bell keeps ringing: duct {n} – {name} is getting too much air.
strings.mg.vent.solved: The bell falls silent. On sheet 3, at the third duct, in my handwriting: “Corridor – waiting room, 14 places”. I calculated the air requirement for fourteen people myself.
strings.mg.vent.hint.1: Tip: every open damper takes air from the other two. The duct to the corridor is twice as long – its damper must stand further open than the typing room’s.
strings.mg.vent.desc.hall: Steel cabinets up to the ceiling, the Süd household index. Cards don’t breathe, but they must stay dry.
strings.mg.vent.desc.typing: Behind glass, the early shift’s typewriters. The night shift gave them all the air.
strings.mg.vent.desc.corridor: The duct runs through the wall beside the waiting bench into the State Police corridor. It is twice as long as the others.
